intro: The minuet makes a dance metre feel weighty and argumentative. Its central Trio changes to G major and divides the conversation between strings and winds before the stern opening returns.
question: Can you keep counting three while the opening phrase seems to pull against the bar lines?

sections.label: Trio · a major-key alternative
sections.mNote: G major; exchanges between instrumental groups

sections.label: Minuet returns
sections.mNote: The minor-key dance returns after the Trio

cues.title: A dance with resistance
cues.text: The minuet begins forcefully, with accents that make the three-beat metre feel less comfortable than a ballroom dance. Listen for the melody pressing across the regular beat instead of merely decorating it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, bars 1–14, PDF p. 30; report begins at high relative level in G minor. The accent pattern is from the score, not the automatic onset estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A summer catalogue
cues.text: Mozart finishes this symphony on 25 July 1788, according to his own thematic catalogue. It belongs to the concentrated summer that also produces his last two other symphonies.
cues.evidence: Marianne Williams Tobias, Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note, Symphony No. 40 (2015), https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. IMSLP work information gives completion on 25 July 1788.

cues.title: The phrase argues back
cues.text: The minuet’s continuation sets short shapes against one another. Imitation gives the inner parts work to do: this is not simply a melody riding over an unchanging dance accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, bars 15–42, PDF pp. 30–31; report has lower relative level at 1:00–1:05, then a stronger span at 1:10–1:30 and boundaries at 1:04 and 1:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The other side of G
cues.text: The central Trio changes G minor to G major and relaxes the texture. Listen for the string phrase and its wind response as a different way of inhabiting the same tonic.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, Trio, bars 43 onward, PDF p. 32; report settles into a quieter G-major region around 1:45, with boundaries at 1:38 and 1:46. The section marker at 1:44 is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Why call it Trio
cues.text: A Classical minuet’s middle section keeps the name “Trio” even when more than three musicians play. Here it identifies the contrasting central dance, not an instruction to reduce the orchestra to three players.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III labels the central section Trio and scores it for changing groups of strings and winds; PDF pp. 32–33.

cues.title: Colour in small groups
cues.text: Through the Trio, notice how the texture changes when a phrase moves from bowed strings to winds. The horns can fill the middle register without making this gentler dance resemble the minuet’s opening attack.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, Trio second strain, PDF pp. 32–33; report 2:40–3:30 remains quieter than the minuet and largely G-major centred. The cue describes the Trio as a whole, not a timed horn entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A return written briefly
cues.text: At the end of the Trio the score says “Menuetto da capo”: return to the beginning of the minuet. Mozart does not need to copy out the opening dance again to make its return part of the design.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, PDF p. 33, final Trio bar: Menuetto da capo.

cues.title: The stern dance returns
cues.text: The G minor minuet is back. Its force is now measured against the gentler music in between; the return restores the opening character rather than gradually transforming the Trio into it.
cues.evidence: Report boundary 3:36 and rise from −22.0 dB at 3:30 to −10.4 dB at 3:40; the score directs a da capo after the Trio. Approximate return marker: 3:34.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hold the three beats
cues.text: Keep the triple pulse under the last phrases. The final chords close the minuet firmly; the symphony still has a separate, faster finale to come.
cues.evidence: Report remains strong around 4:10–4:15, with the recording ending at 4:32.8; score III ends with the returning minuet’s G minor cadence.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

transitions.title: The tonic changes its mode
transitions.how: The minuet closes in G minor. The Trio keeps G as its centre but replaces the minor third with a major third; the strings begin a lighter phrase, answered by winds. A direct change of mode and a reduced texture do the work without a long modulating bridge.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, bars 42–50, PDF pp. 31–32; report lower relative level and G-major region from about 1:45. Marker 1:44 is provisional.

transitions.title: Major gives way to minor
transitions.how: The Trio’s G-major cadence is followed by the instruction to return to the minuet. The strongly accented G-minor tutti replaces the gentler exchanges. The effect depends on direct juxtaposition, not on a gradual increase in tempo or a connecting passage.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, Trio close and Menuetto da capo, PDF p. 33; report rise around 3:35–3:40 and boundary 3:36. Timing is a passage estimate.

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
